learn: Artists develop craft, engage and persist, envision, express, observe, reflect, stretch and explore, and understand the art world.
These habits matter as much as technical skill.
Persistence means working through problems instead of starting over.
check: Studio habits matter as much as...
lessons.try: Rate yourself on each habit and set two goals.

learn: A sketchbook records observations, ideas, experiments and notes.
Daily drawing builds skill and visual memory.
Annotate pages to explain your thinking.
lessons.try: Fill ten sketchbook pages in two weeks with dated, annotated work.

learn: Organise materials, label solvents and ventilate the room.
Use non-toxic materials where possible and read safety labels.
Clean brushes and tools after each session.
lessons.try: Create a studio routine checklist.

learn: A theme is a big idea explored across a body of work: memory, identity, place, change.
Personal connections make themes meaningful.
Artists like Frida Kahlo returned to themes again and again.
lessons.try: Brainstorm thirty possible themes and circle three.

learn: Study artists who explored similar themes.
Gather images, texts and objects as visual research.
Credit sources of inspiration; never copy work as your own.
lessons.try: Make a mood board for your chosen theme.

learn: A series is a group of related works that develop a theme.
Vary media, scale or viewpoint while keeping a common thread.
Plan a series of five to eight pieces.
check: A series is a group of ___ works.
lessons.try: Write a plan for a series of six works.

learn: The adult figure is about seven and a half heads tall.
Gesture drawings (30 seconds to 2 minutes) capture movement and weight.
Look for the line of action through the body.
check: An adult figure is about ___ heads tall.
lessons.try: Do twenty quick gesture drawings from poses or public-domain photos.

learn: Learn major bones and muscles that shape the surface.
Draw the skeleton, then add mass.
Foreshortening shows parts coming toward the viewer.
lessons.try: Draw a hand from three angles.

learn: Eyes sit halfway down the head; the nose ends halfway between eyes and chin.
Small changes in mouth and brows show emotion.
Light and shadow model the face.
check: Eyes sit about ___ down the head.
lessons.try: Draw a self-portrait showing a strong emotion.

learn: Picasso and Braque introduced collage (papier collé) around 1912.
Hannah Höch made photomontages in the Dada movement.
Romare Bearden's collages depicted African American life.
lessons.try: Make a collage from found papers on your theme.

learn: Combine paint, paper, fabric, ink and found objects.
Use appropriate adhesives and seal surfaces.
Layers create depth and history in a work.
lessons.try: Create a mixed-media piece with at least four materials.

learn: Assemblage builds 3D works from found objects.
Joseph Cornell made box assemblages; Louise Nevelson painted wall assemblages one colour.
Objects carry meanings from their past use.
lessons.try: Build a small box assemblage about a memory.

learn: Choose a limited palette to unify a painting.
Temperature (warm and cool) creates depth and mood.
Colour can symbolise ideas.
lessons.try: Paint the same scene with two limited palettes.

learn: Impasto builds thick paint; glazing layers thin transparent colour.
Van Gogh's visible strokes add energy.
Surface texture is part of meaning.
lessons.try: Experiment with impasto and glazing on test panels.

learn: Rule of thirds, leading lines and focal points guide the viewer.
Paintings can tell stories through figures, setting and symbols.
Edit: remove what doesn't serve the idea.
lessons.try: Plan a narrative painting with thumbnail sketches.

learn: Additive: building up (clay, assembly). Subtractive: carving away (stone, wood, soap).
Armatures support additive sculpture.
Consider every viewing angle.
lessons.try: Carve a small form from soap or plaster.

learn: Installations transform a space that viewers enter.
Yayoi Kusama's infinity rooms use mirrors and lights.
Sound, light and scale shape experience.
lessons.try: Design a model of an installation in a shoebox.

learn: Site-specific art responds to a place.
Public art involves communities and permissions.
Land art (Robert Smithson's "Spiral Jetty", 1970) uses the landscape.
lessons.try: Propose a public art piece for your school.

learn: Framing, angle, depth of field and light shape a photo.
Aperture controls depth of field; shutter speed controls motion.
Photographers like Dorothea Lange documented society.
lessons.try: Shoot a photo essay of ten images on your theme.

learn: Editing adjusts exposure, colour and cropping.
Layers and masks allow non-destructive editing.
Be honest about manipulation in documentary images.
lessons.try: Edit a photo non-destructively with layers.

learn: Vector art scales without losing quality; raster art is made of pixels.
Animation creates motion from frames (12 to 24 per second).
Use free tools like Krita, GIMP or Inkscape.
check: Animation often uses ___ frames per second.
lessons.try: Make a short looping animation.

learn: Goya's "The Third of May 1808" (1814) condemned violence.
Picasso's "Guernica" (1937) protested the bombing of a Basque town.
Posters and murals have long been tools of social movements.
lessons.try: Design a poster for a cause you care about.

learn: Who is shown in art and how matters.
Artists such as Kehinde Wiley and Amy Sherald paint Black subjects in powerful ways.
Museums are working to diversify collections.
lessons.try: Analyse who is represented in a museum's collection online.

learn: Copyright protects creators; public domain works are free to use.
Fair use allows limited use for commentary, education and parody.
Creative Commons licences let artists share on their own terms.
lessons.try: Find three public domain artworks and use one in a remix.

learn: Describe, analyse, interpret, evaluate.
Feedback should be kind, specific and helpful.
"I notice... I wonder... What if..." frames feedback.
check: The first critique step is to...
lessons.try: Run a small-group critique using the framework.

learn: Compare work to your intentions and goals.
Identify strengths and areas to improve.
Keep a reflection journal.
lessons.try: Write a reflection on your best and weakest pieces.

learn: Revise by reworking, simplifying or starting a new version.
Document versions to show process.
Knowing when a piece is finished is a skill.
check: Knowing when work is finished is a...
lessons.try: Revise one artwork based on critique and document both versions.

learn: Curators choose and arrange works to create meaning.
Sequence, spacing and lighting shape the viewer's path.
Hang work with centres about 57-60 inches from the floor.
check: Centres are often hung about ___ from the floor.
lessons.try: Plan the layout of a small exhibition.

learn: A statement explains your theme, process and intent in clear language.
Avoid jargon; write in the first person.
Keep it to one to three paragraphs.
lessons.try: Write an artist statement for your series.

learn: A portfolio shows your best and most varied work.
Photograph work in even light against neutral backgrounds.
Careers include fine art, design, illustration, animation, teaching and curating.
lessons.try: Assemble a digital portfolio of twelve pieces.
